implementation_notes: The modern default: a positional record (or a record with init-only properties) is the DTO, and System.Text.Json - in-box since .NET Core 3.0 - serialises it directly, using the parameterised constructor for deserialisation, so no mutable state and no parameterless constructor are needed. The record replaces the classic get/set bean and its equals/hashCode/toString boilerplate at once. Keep a class instead only when a legacy serializer, model binder or ORM demands a parameterless constructor plus settable properties.
pitfalls: Constructor binding is name-based and case-sensitive by default: a JSON key that does not match the parameter/property name silently yields the default value unless a naming policy or [JsonPropertyName] is configured.
Records are only shallowly immutable - a mutable array or list member can still be modified after construction.
Structural equality makes two value-equal records interchangeable as dictionary keys and breaks reference-identity assumptions (caching, lookups).

variants.name: Mutable DTO class with parameterless constructor (classic)
variants.idiom_name: public class with auto-properties and a no-arg constructor
variants.implementation_notes: The classic realization still required by parts of the .NET ecosystem: XML serializers, model binding and some ORMs need a public parameterless constructor and settable (or init-only) properties, so the DTO is a mutable class with auto-properties, optionally with required members. It keeps maximum tool compatibility at the price of pointless mutation potential and no value equality. Choose it when a framework contract demands it, not by default.
pitfalls: Mutable DTOs can be rewritten by any holder between production and consumption; treat them as read-only once assembled.
Property initializers run per instance, but caching or reusing one DTO instance (static, DI singleton) leaks state across requests.
